transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-01-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Aisha (Redwood SE), Lena (CTO, SilverShore), Imran (Cloud Ops), Ruth (Security), Tom (ML)

Summary:
Quick kickoff to scope a private-network POC. Main goals: ensure data never leaves region, validate latency/throughput for their genomics model workload, and confirm connectivity approach (federated VPC via Transit / PrivateLink endpoints). Agree next steps for bench runs and landing zone creation.

Topics: Success criteria, workload sizing, benchmarking plan, VPC peering vs PrivateLink tradeoffs, egress constraints, timeline

Action items (mentioned verbally during call): see metadata list above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick intros real quick. imaya maya chen redwood, im the AE on this account. diego and aisha are our se leads.
[00:12] Lena: hey all, lena here, CTO at silver shore bio, thanks for making time. we're trying to get a pilot up to validate residency and perf for a genomics annotation model.
[00:23] Diego: great, can you walk me through the top success criteria? what would make this POC a win for you?
[00:30] Tom: sure, our primary is residency: all inference must remain in the customer's region, no public egress. second is latency—sub 300ms p95 for typical inference (prompt ~256 tokens), and finally throughput we want to reach ~30 concurrent requests sustained during peak jobs.
[00:51] Aisha: and just to confirm, you want both eu-west-1 and us-east-1 covered in the pilot?
[00:58] Imran: yes, those two regions initially. long term we'll add ap-southeast but that's later. also we have strict egress rules, e.g., no internet NATing for inference traffic, only controlled egress via our egress gateway with firewall rules.
[01:15] Ruth: from security perspective we need KMS integration (customer-managed keys), audit logs forwarded to our Splunk, and proof that model artifacts and inference logs don't transit other regions. SOC2 plus additional biotech controls.
[01:30] Diego: ok makes sense. we typically support two private connectivity patterns: VPC peering / transit gateway based federation, or interface endpoints via PrivateLink. both can meet residency but they have different operational and egress characteristics.
[01:46] Maya: i'll pivot to the tradeoffs quickly—peering/transit gives flatter network path and lower latency but requires more routing and potentially cross-account route propagation; privatelink isolates via endpoints and keeps traffic on AWS backbone but can add request hop and has endpoint quotas and costs.
[02:06] Lena: can you quantify the added latency for PrivateLink vs peering?
[02:10] Diego: ballpark, we've seen an extra 10-40ms depending on region and path; for short inference it can be noticeable at p95. peering/transit is generally lowest latency, especially within region. that said, PrivateLink reduces surface area for security because you control endpoint policies per-service.
[02:29] Imran: we also need DNS hygiene. if we do privatelink, we'll need private hosted zones and split-horizon DNS. can redwood handle that?
[02:37] Aisha: yep we can provide guidance. our private control plane supports private route records and we give a sample zone configuration in the reference diagram.
[02:45] Tom: about benchmarks—what's the typical bench you run?
[02:49] Diego: we recommend a three-step bench: synthetic latency sweep, concurrency ramp to find throughput/KV cache behavior, and an end-to-end dataset run with ~1k real payloads. for your workload we propose: 1) single-request p95/p99 sweep with 256 token prompts, 2) 60s sustained concurrency ramps to 30-60 concurrent sessions, 3) 3 x 5 minute runs measuring CPU/GPU utilization, token/sec and token cost.
[03:20] Lena: and how many total requests should we expect for the POC?
[03:24] Diego: typical POC uses ~10k synthetic requests across runs; if you want more realism we can run 50k but that'll take longer and cost more.
[03:32] Ruth: cost is a concern, we need an estimate for both privatelink and peering setups, plus the Dedicated reserved pilot vs hosted-with-private-connect options.
[03:42] Maya: i'll prepare a short pricing estimator showing a 2-week small reserved pool vs hosted with privatelink egress. i'll include expected token costs for the benchmark volume.
[03:52] Imran: one constraint—our accounts are locked down, we cannot accept incoming VPC peering without a change control ticket. we usually prefer PrivateLink for easier approvals.
[04:03] Diego: noted. private link does avoid the peering change control but remember endpoints are regional — so you'll need an endpoint per region for us-east-1 and eu-west-1. also watch for interface endpoint ENI IP consumption on small subnets.
[04:19] Tom: about KV cache—do you support hot prefix caching so repeated queries are faster? for our use case we have repeated reference queries during a pipeline.
[04:28] Aisha: yes, we have KV cache and prefix caching; in Dedicated mode we can pin cache to a GPU pool to improve hit rates. we'll measure cache hit rate during the bench.
[04:39] Lena: what about private deployment options—can we run a private control plane within our VPC?
[04:44] Diego: we offer a Private deployment model where control plane sits in your VPC or a customer-managed account and inference happens on dedicated pools. that model addresses strong residency needs but has longer ramp and higher ops cost. for POC we usually do hosted control plane with PrivateLink back to customer's VPC, then evaluate full Private deployment if needed.
[05:04] Ruth: and encryption at rest? keys must be our KMS, no Redwood-managed keys.
[05:09] Aisha: supported — we integrate with customer KMS and can support HSM-backed keys for model artifacts. we'll include the KMS integration steps in the doc.
[05:18] Maya: ok, timeline. if we start now: week 1 - landing zone + endpoint provisioning; week 2 - baseline bench run (single region), week 3 - multi-region bench and egress policy validation, week 4 - results review and next steps. so about 3-4 weeks to a complete POC.
[05:35] Imran: that fits our schedule, though we need approval for any cross-account resource changes; again PrivateLink preferred.
[05:43] Diego: for the bench we'll need three things from you: test data (or a synthetic generator), account IDs/subnets for endpoints, and a list of prompt templates. Tom, can you own the prompt set?
[05:56] Tom: yes i'll assemble 500 templates that represent our pipeline and share them in a google bucket.
[06:02] Lena: on success criteria—let's be explicit: 1) no egress to public internet confirmed by flow logs, 2) p95 latency <300ms for 256 token prompts, p99 <450ms, 3) sustained 30 concurrent sessions with <5% error rate, 4) KMS-managed keys and audit logs to Splunk.
[06:24] Maya: perfect we'll use those as the acceptance criteria. we'll tag the bench runs to measure each item.
[06:29] Ruth: one more ask—can you prove that model artifacts won't be replicated outside the region? we need a short write-up.
[06:35] Aisha: yes we'll include a data flow diagram and a short affidavit of regional storage behavior for the POC.
[06:41] Maya: final logistics: i'll send the reference architecture (federated-VPC diagram), Diego will prepare the bench harness, and we'll aim to kick off the landing zone setup by 2028-01-23. next meeting to review readiness will be 2028-01-27.
[06:58] Lena: thanks all sounds good.
[07:02] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and calendar invites.

End of transcript.
